topics.name: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
topics.question: What is Artificial Intelligence?
topics.definition: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the field of computer science that builds systems able to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as perceiving, reasoning, learning, planning, understanding language and making decisions.
topics.simple: AI is about making computers do things that usually need human thinking. Instead of following only fixed step-by-step rules, an AI system can recognise patterns, make decisions and sometimes learn from experience. When your phone unlocks by recognising your face, or a map app finds the fastest route, that is AI at work.
topics.eli10: Imagine teaching a robot to play a game. At first it knows nothing, but you show it lots of games and it slowly figures out which moves are good. AI is the science of making computers smart like that, so they can spot things, solve puzzles and make choices a bit like people do.
topics.analogy: Think of AI as a new employee. Rule-based AI is an employee who follows a thick instruction manual exactly. Machine-learning AI is an employee who watches thousands of examples of experienced colleagues and learns the patterns on their own. Both get the job done, but the second one can handle situations the manual never described.
how_it_works: Define the task and how success is measured (for example, accuracy of a diagnosis).
Represent the problem: states and actions for search, facts and rules for reasoning, or features for learning.
Choose an approach: search and planning, logical reasoning, probabilistic models or machine learning.
Build or train the system on knowledge or data.
Evaluate it on new situations and improve it.
topics.example: A spam filter is a classic AI system. It looks at features of an email (words used, sender, links) and decides whether it is spam. A modern filter is trained on millions of emails labelled 'spam' or 'not spam', so it learns patterns such as 'contains "urgent prize" and a suspicious link' without a programmer writing every rule.
applications: Healthcare: medical image analysis and diagnosis support
Transport: route planning and driver-assistance systems
Language: translation, chatbots and speech recognition
Finance: fraud detection and credit scoring
Recommendation systems on streaming and shopping platforms
advantages: Automates repetitive and large-scale decision tasks
Can find patterns in data that are too large for humans to analyse
Works continuously and consistently
limitations: Learned systems can inherit bias from their training data
Many models are hard to interpret (black boxes)
Systems can fail in situations very different from what they were built or trained for
key_points: AI builds systems that perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence.
Narrow AI solves specific tasks; general AI (human-level on all tasks) does not yet exist.
Main approaches: search, knowledge-based reasoning, probabilistic reasoning and machine learning.
Machine learning is a subset of AI; deep learning is a subset of machine learning.
The Turing Test is a classic proposal for judging machine intelligence through conversation.
viva: Define Artificial Intelligence.
AI is the branch of computer science concerned with building systems that perform tasks requiring human intelligence, such as reasoning, learning, perception and decision making.
What is the difference between narrow AI and general AI?
Narrow AI is designed for one specific task, like playing chess or recognising faces. General AI would match human ability across any intellectual task; it does not exist yet.
How are AI, ML and DL related?
They are nested: machine learning is a subset of AI that learns from data, and deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses multi-layer neural networks.
What is the Turing Test?
Proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, it says a machine can be considered intelligent if a human judge, chatting by text, cannot reliably tell it apart from a human.
Give two ethical concerns in AI.
Bias and unfairness learned from data, and lack of transparency or accountability in automated decisions. Privacy is another major concern.
interview: How would you explain the difference between AI and machine learning to a non-technical manager?

AI is the overall goal of making machines act intelligently. Machine learning is one way of achieving it: instead of programming every rule, we give the system many examples and it learns the rules itself. So all machine learning is AI, but not all AI is machine learning; a hand-written chess engine is AI without learning.
What are the main risks of deploying an AI system in production?

Data drift, where real-world data changes and accuracy drops; bias that leads to unfair outcomes; lack of explainability for regulated decisions; security issues like adversarial inputs; and over-reliance by users. I would mitigate these with monitoring, fairness checks, human review for high-stakes decisions and regular retraining.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between AI, ML and DL?
options: DL is a subset of ML, which is a subset of AI
AI is a subset of ML
ML is a subset of DL
mcqs.explanation: Deep learning is a type of machine learning, and machine learning is one approach to AI.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of narrow AI?
mcqs.explanation: A chess program is specialised for one task, which is the definition of narrow AI.

mcqs.q: Who proposed the Turing Test?
mcqs.explanation: Alan Turing proposed the 'imitation game' in his 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'.

topics.name: Intelligent Agents
topics.question: What is an intelligent agent?
topics.definition: An intelligent agent is anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts on that environment through actuators, choosing actions that maximise its expected performance measure.
topics.simple: An agent is something that can sense what is around it and then do something about it. A robot vacuum is a good example: it senses dirt and walls, and it decides where to move and when to suck. It is called 'intelligent' when it picks actions that help it reach its goal, like cleaning the whole room quickly.
topics.eli10: Think of a robot vacuum. It has 'eyes' (sensors) to notice dirt and walls, and 'hands and feet' (wheels and a brush) to move and clean. It keeps looking around and deciding what to do next. Anything that notices things and then acts to reach a goal is called an agent.
topics.analogy: An intelligent agent is like a thermostat with a brain. A simple thermostat senses the temperature and switches the heater on or off (a simple reflex agent). A smart thermostat also remembers your routine, predicts when you will come home and plans heating in advance to save energy (a goal- and utility-based agent).
how_it_works: Percept: the agent receives input from sensors (camera, text, temperature).
Agent function: maps the history of percepts to an action.
The agent program implements this function, possibly using internal state, goals or a utility function.
Actuators carry out the chosen action, which changes the environment.
The cycle repeats: perceive, decide, act.
topics.example: A self-driving car is an agent. Its sensors are cameras, radar and GPS; its actuators are the steering, accelerator and brakes. Its performance measure includes safety, reaching the destination, speed and passenger comfort. Its environment is partially observable, dynamic, continuous and multi-agent, which makes it very challenging.
applications: Robot vacuum cleaners and warehouse robots
Game-playing agents such as chess and Go engines
Software agents like web crawlers and trading bots
Virtual assistants that plan and carry out tasks
advantages: Gives a unified framework to describe any AI system
Separates the environment, percepts, actions and goals clearly
Scales from simple reflex behaviour to learning agents
limitations: Designing a correct performance measure is hard
Partially observable, dynamic environments make decisions uncertain
Simple reflex agents fail when the right action depends on history
key_points: Agent = architecture + program; it perceives via sensors and acts via actuators.
PEAS describes a task: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors.
Agent types: simple reflex, model-based reflex, goal-based, utility-based and learning agents.
Environment properties: observable, deterministic, episodic, static, discrete, single/multi-agent.
A rational agent chooses the action expected to maximise its performance measure.
viva: What is PEAS?
PEAS stands for Performance measure, Environment, Actuators and Sensors. It is used to specify the task environment of an agent.
What is a rational agent?
A rational agent selects the action that is expected to maximise its performance measure, given its percepts and built-in knowledge.
Name the five types of agents.
Simple reflex, model-based reflex, goal-based, utility-based and learning agents.
What is the difference between a goal-based and a utility-based agent?
A goal-based agent only checks whether a goal is reached. A utility-based agent measures how good each state is, so it can choose between several ways of reaching the goal.
What does 'partially observable' mean?
The agent's sensors cannot see the complete state of the environment at each moment, so it must keep an internal model or memory.
interview: Describe the PEAS for an automated taxi.

Performance: safety, legal driving, reaching the destination, speed, comfort and profit. Environment: roads, traffic, pedestrians, weather and customers. Actuators: steering, accelerator, brake, horn and display. Sensors: cameras, lidar/radar, GPS, speedometer, odometer and microphones.
Why is a simple reflex agent not enough for most real problems?

It only reacts to the current percept using condition-action rules, so it fails when the environment is partially observable or when the correct action depends on the past. Model-based agents fix this by keeping internal state, and goal- or utility-based agents add planning.

mcqs.q: In PEAS, what does the 'A' stand for?
mcqs.explanation: PEAS = Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors.

mcqs.q: Which agent type keeps an internal state to handle partially observable environments?
mcqs.explanation: A model-based agent maintains an internal model of the world that tracks parts it cannot currently see.

topics.name: Search Algorithms in AI
topics.question: What are search algorithms in AI?
topics.definition: Search algorithms solve problems by systematically exploring a state space: starting from an initial state, they apply actions to generate new states until they reach a goal state, ideally along the lowest-cost path.
topics.simple: Many AI problems can be turned into 'find a path' problems. A maze, a route on a map or a puzzle all have a start, a goal and possible moves. A search algorithm tries moves in an organised way until it finds the goal. Uninformed searches such as BFS and DFS explore blindly, while informed searches such as A* use a hint (a heuristic) about which direction looks promising.
topics.eli10: Imagine you lost your ball somewhere in a big house. You could check every room one floor at a time (that is like breadth-first search), or go as deep as possible down one hallway before coming back (depth-first search). If you hear the dog barking near the ball, you can use that clue to look in the best rooms first. That clue is what AI calls a heuristic.
topics.analogy: Search is like finding a route in a new city. BFS is checking every street one block away, then two blocks away, and so on. DFS is following one road as far as it goes before turning back. A* is using a map that tells you the straight-line distance to your destination, so you always try the street that looks closest overall.
how_it_works: Formulate the problem: initial state, actions, transition model, goal test and path cost.
Put the initial state in the frontier (the list of states waiting to be explored).
Repeatedly pick a state from the frontier; BFS uses a queue, DFS a stack, UCS and A* a priority queue.
If it is the goal, return the path; otherwise expand it and add its unseen neighbours to the frontier.
A* orders the frontier by f(n) = g(n) + h(n): cost so far plus estimated cost to the goal.
topics.example: Find a route from city A to city D. Roads: A-B (1), A-C (4), B-C (2), B-D (5), C-D (1). BFS finds A-B-D or A-C-D (fewest edges) but ignores cost. Uniform-cost search expands the cheapest path first and finds A-B-C-D with cost 1+2+1 = 4, which is optimal. A* with an admissible heuristic finds the same optimal path while expanding fewer nodes.
applications: GPS navigation and route planning
Puzzle solving (8-puzzle, Rubik's cube, Sudoku)
Game playing using minimax and alpha-beta pruning
Robot motion planning and scheduling
advantages: General: many problems can be framed as search
BFS and UCS are complete and optimal under standard conditions
Heuristics (A*) can reduce the explored space dramatically
limitations: State spaces can grow exponentially with depth (combinatorial explosion)
BFS needs a lot of memory; DFS may not find the shortest path
A* is only as good as its heuristic
key_points: Uninformed search (BFS, DFS, UCS, iterative deepening) uses no domain knowledge.
Informed search (greedy best-first, A*) uses a heuristic h(n).
A* uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n) and is optimal if h is admissible (never overestimates).
BFS is complete and optimal for equal step costs; DFS uses little memory but is not optimal.
Adversarial search (minimax, alpha-beta) is used for two-player games.
viva: What is the difference between BFS and DFS?

BFS explores level by level using a queue and finds the shallowest goal; DFS goes as deep as possible along one branch using a stack and uses less memory but is not guaranteed to find the shortest path.
What is a heuristic?
A heuristic is an estimate of the cost from a state to the nearest goal, used to guide informed search towards promising states.
When is A* optimal?
A* tree search is optimal when the heuristic is admissible, meaning it never overestimates the true cost. For graph search the heuristic should also be consistent.
What is alpha-beta pruning?
An optimisation of minimax that skips branches that cannot affect the final decision, giving the same result with fewer node evaluations.
What is iterative deepening search?
It runs depth-limited DFS with increasing depth limits. It combines the low memory of DFS with the completeness of BFS.
interview: Why is A* preferred over Dijkstra's algorithm for route finding on a map?

Both find optimal paths, but Dijkstra expands nodes in all directions based only on cost so far. A* adds a heuristic such as straight-line distance to the destination, so it focuses on nodes that lead towards the goal and usually expands far fewer nodes, while staying optimal if the heuristic is admissible.
What are the time and space complexities of BFS?

With branching factor b and solution depth d, BFS takes O(b^d) time and O(b^d) space, because it stores the whole frontier. Memory is usually the bottleneck, which is why iterative deepening is often preferred.

mcqs.q: Which data structure does BFS use for its frontier?
mcqs.explanation: BFS processes states in first-in first-out order, which a queue provides.

mcqs.q: In A*, what does f(n) = g(n) + h(n) represent?
options: Cost so far plus estimated cost to goal
mcqs.explanation: g(n) is the path cost from the start to n and h(n) estimates the remaining cost from n to the goal.

mcqs.q: A heuristic that never overestimates the true cost is called:
mcqs.explanation: Admissible heuristics guarantee A* tree search returns an optimal solution.

numerical.problem: A* search: node n has path cost g(n) = 7 and heuristic h(n) = 5; node m has g(m) = 9 and h(m) = 2. Which node does A* expand first?
numerical.solution:
Step 1: f(n) = g(n) + h(n) = 7 + 5 = 12.
Step 2: f(m) = 9 + 2 = 11.
Step 3: A* expands the node with the smallest f value.
Answer: node m is expanded first, because 11 < 12, even though it has a higher cost so far.

topics.name: Knowledge Representation
topics.question: What is knowledge representation in AI?
topics.definition: Knowledge representation (KR) is the part of AI concerned with storing information about the world in a form a computer can use to reason, answer questions and solve problems. Common forms are logic, rules, semantic networks, frames and ontologies.
topics.simple: A computer cannot reason about the world unless the facts are written down in a structured way. Knowledge representation is choosing that structure. For example, 'All humans are mortal' and 'Socrates is a human' can be written in logic so the computer can conclude 'Socrates is mortal'.
topics.eli10: Imagine making a family tree on paper. You draw boxes for people and lines showing who is whose parent. Now you can answer questions like 'Who is my cousin?' by following the lines. Knowledge representation is making 'family trees' like this for computers, so they can figure things out.
topics.analogy: Knowledge representation is like a library's cataloguing system. The books (facts) are only useful if they are organised with titles, categories and cross-references. A good catalogue lets a librarian quickly answer 'which books are about birds that cannot fly?', just as a good representation lets an AI system reason efficiently.
how_it_works: Identify the objects, properties and relationships in the domain.
Choose a formalism: propositional/first-order logic, production rules, semantic networks, frames or ontologies.
Encode facts (e.g. Bird(Tweety)) and rules (e.g. Bird(x) -> CanFly(x)).
Use an inference engine (forward or backward chaining, resolution) to derive new facts.
Answer queries and explain the chain of reasoning.
topics.example: In first-order logic: Human(Socrates) and for all x, Human(x) -> Mortal(x). Using the rule Modus Ponens, the system infers Mortal(Socrates). In a semantic network, the same knowledge is a node 'Socrates' linked by an 'is-a' edge to 'Human', which has the property 'mortal', so the property is inherited.
applications: Expert systems for medical or technical diagnosis
Knowledge graphs used by search engines
Ontologies in the semantic web and biomedicine
Planning systems and question answering
advantages: Reasoning is explainable: you can trace which rules were used
Knowledge can be edited directly by experts
Works with little or no training data
limitations: Manually encoding knowledge is slow (the knowledge acquisition bottleneck)
Handling uncertainty and exceptions is difficult in pure logic
Very expressive logics can make inference computationally expensive
key_points: KR stores knowledge so a machine can reason with it.
Main formalisms: logic, production rules, semantic networks, frames, ontologies.
Inference methods: forward chaining (data-driven) and backward chaining (goal-driven).
First-order logic adds objects, predicates and quantifiers to propositional logic.
Knowledge graphs are a modern, large-scale form of semantic networks.
viva: What is the difference between propositional and first-order logic?

Propositional logic works with whole statements that are true or false. First-order logic adds objects, predicates, functions and quantifiers (for all, there exists), so it can express general rules about many objects.
What is forward chaining?
A data-driven inference method that starts from known facts and applies rules to derive new facts until the goal is reached or nothing new can be inferred.
What is backward chaining?
A goal-driven method that starts from the goal and works backwards, looking for rules and facts that can prove it. Prolog uses backward chaining.
What is a semantic network?
A graph where nodes represent concepts or objects and labelled edges represent relationships such as is-a or has-part.
What is a frame?
A structured record representing a stereotyped object or situation, with slots (attributes) and default values, such as a 'Restaurant' frame with slots for menu and bill.
interview: When would you choose a knowledge-based approach over machine learning?

When there is little labelled data, when decisions must be fully explainable or auditable, or when the rules are well known and stable, as in tax rules or regulatory checks. In practice, hybrid systems are common, for example a knowledge graph combined with a learned language model.
What is a knowledge graph?

A knowledge graph stores entities as nodes and relationships as labelled edges, such as (Paris, capitalOf, France). It supports queries and reasoning over connected facts and is used in search engines, recommendation and retrieval-augmented LLM systems.

mcqs.q: Which inference method starts from the goal and works backwards?
mcqs.explanation: Backward chaining is goal-driven; forward chaining is data-driven.

mcqs.q: Which representation uses nodes and labelled edges such as 'is-a'?
mcqs.explanation: Semantic networks are graphs of concepts connected by relationships.

topics.name: Supervised Learning
topics.question: What is supervised learning?
topics.definition: Supervised learning is a type of machine learning in which a model learns a mapping from inputs X to outputs y using a labelled dataset, so that it can predict the label for new, unseen inputs.
topics.simple: In supervised learning we teach the computer with examples that already have the right answers. For instance, we show it thousands of house descriptions together with their prices. It learns the relationship, and later it can guess the price of a house it has never seen. If the answer is a number, it is regression; if it is a category, it is classification.
topics.eli10: It is like learning with flashcards. One side shows a picture of an animal, the other side says 'cat' or 'dog'. After practising with many cards, you can name animals on new cards you have never seen. The computer learns the same way, from examples that come with the right answer.
topics.analogy: Supervised learning is like a student practising with a solved question bank. Every question comes with the correct answer, so after each attempt the student checks, notices mistakes and adjusts. The labels play the role of the teacher's answer key.
how_it_works: Collect a labelled dataset of (input, correct output) pairs.
Split it into training, validation and test sets.
Choose a model (linear regression, decision tree, neural network...) and a loss function.
Train: adjust model parameters to minimise the loss between predictions and labels.
Tune hyper-parameters on the validation set and report final performance on the test set.
topics.example: Email spam detection: inputs are emails, labels are 'spam' or 'not spam'. A logistic regression or naive Bayes model learns which word patterns indicate spam. On a test set of 1,000 unseen emails it might correctly classify 970, giving 97% accuracy.
applications: Spam filtering and sentiment analysis (classification)
House price and sales forecasting (regression)
Medical diagnosis from images or test results
Credit scoring and fraud detection
advantages: Clear objective and easy-to-measure performance
Usually more accurate than unsupervised methods when labels exist
Many mature algorithms and tools
limitations: Needs labelled data, which can be expensive to create
Label noise or bias is learned by the model
May not generalise to data that differs from the training distribution
key_points: Supervised learning learns from labelled (input, output) pairs.
Two main tasks: regression (continuous output) and classification (discrete output).
Training minimises a loss function such as MSE or cross-entropy.
Data is split into train, validation and test sets to measure generalisation.
Common algorithms: linear/logistic regression, decision trees, SVM, KNN, neural networks.
viva: What is labelled data?
Data where every input comes with the correct output, for example an image tagged 'cat'.
What are the two main types of supervised learning?
Regression, which predicts continuous values, and classification, which predicts discrete classes.
Why do we need a separate test set?
To estimate how well the model performs on unseen data. Evaluating on training data would overestimate performance.
What is a loss function?
A function that measures how far the model's predictions are from the true labels; training tries to minimise it.
Give two supervised learning algorithms.
Linear regression and decision trees. Others include SVM, KNN, logistic regression and neural networks.
interview: How do you decide between a regression and a classification formulation?

By the target variable. If it is a continuous quantity like price or temperature, it is regression. If it is a category like fraud/not fraud, it is classification. Sometimes a problem can be framed either way, for example predicting a rating as a number or as a class, and the choice depends on how the prediction will be used and evaluated.
What would you do if you have very few labels?

Use transfer learning from a pre-trained model, data augmentation, semi-supervised or self-supervised learning, active learning to label the most informative examples, and simpler models with regularisation to avoid overfitting.

mcqs.q: Predicting a house price from its size is an example of:
mcqs.explanation: The output is a continuous number, which makes it a regression task.

mcqs.q: What does supervised learning require?
mcqs.explanation: Supervised learning needs inputs paired with correct outputs.

topics.name: Unsupervised Learning
topics.question: What is unsupervised learning?
topics.definition: Unsupervised learning is a type of machine learning that finds structure in data without labels, for example grouping similar items (clustering), reducing the number of features (dimensionality reduction) or detecting unusual points (anomaly detection).
topics.simple: In unsupervised learning, we give the computer data but no correct answers. Its job is to discover patterns on its own. For example, a shop can give it customer purchase data, and it may discover groups such as 'budget shoppers' and 'luxury shoppers' even though nobody told it those groups exist.
topics.eli10: Imagine you get a big box of mixed LEGO pieces and nobody tells you anything. You might sort them into piles by colour or by shape all by yourself. Unsupervised learning is the computer sorting things into groups without being told the answers.
topics.analogy: Unsupervised learning is like a new librarian receiving thousands of unlabelled books. Without a catalogue, they start grouping books that share similar words and themes. Later they notice the groups correspond to 'history', 'science' and 'cooking', but the grouping came first, without labels.
how_it_works: Collect unlabelled data and scale the features so distances are meaningful.
Choose a goal: clustering, dimensionality reduction, density estimation or anomaly detection.
Apply an algorithm such as K-Means, DBSCAN, hierarchical clustering, PCA or autoencoders.
Evaluate with internal measures (e.g. silhouette score) and domain inspection.
Interpret and use the discovered structure, e.g. for segmentation or as features.
topics.example: Customer segmentation: an online store has spending and visit-frequency data for 10,000 customers. K-Means with k = 4 finds groups such as frequent low spenders, rare high spenders, loyal high spenders and inactive customers. Marketing can then design a campaign for each group.
applications: Customer segmentation
Anomaly and fraud detection
Dimensionality reduction for visualisation (PCA, t-SNE)
Topic modelling of documents
advantages: No need for expensive labels
Can reveal hidden structure that humans did not expect
Useful as a preprocessing step for supervised learning
limitations: Hard to evaluate because there is no ground truth
Results depend strongly on feature scaling and hyper-parameters like k
Discovered groups may not be meaningful for the business problem
key_points: Unsupervised learning works with unlabelled data.
Main tasks: clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, density estimation.
Algorithms: K-Means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN, PCA, autoencoders.
Evaluation uses internal metrics like silhouette score or inspection by experts.
Self-supervised learning (used to pre-train LLMs) creates labels from the data itself.
viva: How does unsupervised learning differ from supervised learning?
Supervised learning uses labelled examples to learn an input-output mapping; unsupervised learning has no labels and discovers structure in the data.
Name two unsupervised learning tasks.
Clustering and dimensionality reduction. Anomaly detection is another.
What is PCA used for?
Principal Component Analysis reduces the number of features by projecting data onto the directions of maximum variance.
How can you evaluate a clustering result?
With internal metrics such as the silhouette score or Davies-Bouldin index, and by checking whether the clusters make sense to domain experts.
interview: Give a real business use case of unsupervised learning.

Fraud detection in banking: most transactions are unlabelled, so we model normal behaviour with clustering or an isolation forest and flag transactions that are far from normal patterns. Analysts then review the flagged cases, which can also produce labels for a later supervised model.
What is the difference between unsupervised and self-supervised learning?

Unsupervised learning finds structure without any targets. Self-supervised learning creates targets automatically from the data, such as predicting the next word or a masked word, and then trains like supervised learning. LLM pre-training is self-supervised.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an unsupervised learning algorithm?
mcqs.explanation: K-Means groups unlabelled data into clusters.

mcqs.q: PCA is mainly used for:
mcqs.explanation: PCA projects data onto fewer dimensions that keep most of the variance.

topics.name: Regression (Linear Regression)
topics.question: What is regression in machine learning?
topics.definition: Regression is a supervised learning task that predicts a continuous numerical value. Linear regression, the simplest form, models the target as a weighted sum of the input features plus a bias: y = w1*x1 + ... + wn*xn + b.
topics.simple: Regression is used when the answer is a number, like a price, a temperature or a salary. Linear regression draws the best straight line through the data points. 'Best' means the line with the smallest total squared distance between the predicted values and the real values.
topics.eli10: Imagine you notice that the more hours you practise football, the more goals you score. If you draw your results on graph paper and put a ruler through the middle of the dots, you can guess how many goals you would score after practising for 10 hours. That ruler line is linear regression.
topics.analogy: Linear regression is like adjusting a rubber band stretched across pins on a board. Each pin is a data point pulling on the band. The band settles where the total pull (the squared error) is smallest, which is the best-fit line.
how_it_works: Model: y_hat = w*x + b (or a weighted sum of many features).
Loss: Mean Squared Error, MSE = (1/n) * sum((y - y_hat)^2).
Find w and b that minimise MSE, either with the closed-form normal equation or with gradient descent.
Evaluate using MSE, RMSE, MAE or R-squared on test data.
Extensions: polynomial regression, Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1) regularisation.
topics.example: Predicting house price from size: after training, the model is price = 3,000 * size + 50,000. A 1,200 sq ft house is predicted at 3,000 * 1,200 + 50,000 = 3,650,000. The weight 3,000 means each extra square foot adds about 3,000 to the price.
applications: House price prediction
Sales and demand forecasting
Estimating crop yield from rainfall and fertiliser
Predicting a student's marks from study hours
advantages: Simple, fast and easy to interpret
Coefficients show how each feature affects the prediction
Works well when the relationship is roughly linear
limitations: Cannot capture non-linear relationships without feature engineering
Sensitive to outliers because errors are squared
Assumes features are not strongly correlated (multicollinearity causes unstable weights)
key_points: Regression predicts continuous values.
Linear regression: y = wx + b, trained by minimising Mean Squared Error.
Solved by the normal equation or gradient descent.
Metrics: MSE, RMSE, MAE and R-squared.
Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1) add regularisation to reduce overfitting.
viva: What loss function does linear regression use?
Mean Squared Error, the average of the squared differences between predicted and actual values.
What does R-squared measure?
The proportion of variance in the target explained by the model; 1 means a perfect fit, 0 means no better than predicting the mean.
What is the difference between Lasso and Ridge regression?
Ridge adds an L2 penalty that shrinks weights; Lasso adds an L1 penalty that can shrink some weights exactly to zero, performing feature selection.
Why is linear regression sensitive to outliers?
Because errors are squared, a single point far from the line has a very large influence on the loss.
interview: What are the assumptions of linear regression?

Linearity between features and target, independence of errors, homoscedasticity (constant error variance), normally distributed residuals for inference, and no strong multicollinearity among features.
How would you handle a non-linear relationship in a regression problem?

Add polynomial or interaction features, transform variables (for example a log transform), or switch to a non-linear model such as a decision tree ensemble or a neural network, while checking validation error to avoid overfitting.

mcqs.q: Which metric is commonly minimised when training linear regression?
mcqs.explanation: Linear regression minimises the mean of squared residuals.

mcqs.q: Which regularisation can set some weights exactly to zero?
mcqs.explanation: The L1 penalty produces sparse solutions.

numerical.problem: A linear regression model is y = 2x + 1. For the data points (1, 4), (2, 5) and (3, 6), calculate the Mean Squared Error.
numerical.solution:
Step 1: Predictions: x=1 -> 3, x=2 -> 5, x=3 -> 7.
Step 2: Errors (y - y_hat): 4-3 = 1, 5-5 = 0, 6-7 = -1.
Step 3: Squared errors: 1, 0, 1.
Step 4: MSE = (1 + 0 + 1) / 3 = 0.667.
Answer: MSE is approximately 0.67.

topics.name: Classification
topics.question: What is classification in machine learning?
topics.definition: Classification is a supervised learning task that assigns an input to one of a set of discrete classes, such as spam/not spam or cat/dog/bird. Models usually output a probability for each class and pick the most likely one.
topics.simple: Classification is when the answer is a category rather than a number. Is this email spam or not? Is this tumour benign or malignant? The model learns from labelled examples and draws a boundary that separates the classes. Logistic regression, decision trees, SVMs and neural networks are common classifiers.
topics.eli10: Think of sorting fruit into baskets: apples in one, bananas in another. You look at the colour, shape and size to decide. A classification model does the same: it looks at the features of something and decides which basket it belongs in.
topics.analogy: A classifier is like a post office sorting machine. Each letter (input) is examined for clues such as the postcode, and dropped into the right bin (class). The machine learned the rules by seeing many letters that were already sorted correctly.
how_it_works: Collect labelled examples for each class.
Train a model that outputs class scores or probabilities (e.g. sigmoid for binary, softmax for multi-class).
Minimise cross-entropy loss between predicted probabilities and true labels.
Predict the class with the highest probability, or apply a decision threshold.
Evaluate with accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score and the confusion matrix.
topics.example: A disease test classifier is evaluated on 100 patients: TP = 40, FN = 10, FP = 5, TN = 45. Accuracy = (40+45)/100 = 85%. Precision = 40/(40+5) = 0.89. Recall = 40/(40+10) = 0.80. For a disease screening test, recall matters most because missing a sick patient is costly.
applications: Spam and phishing detection
Medical diagnosis
Image recognition
Sentiment analysis of reviews
advantages: Directly answers yes/no or category questions
Probabilistic outputs allow adjustable thresholds
Wide choice of algorithms for different data types
limitations: Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced datasets
Needs enough labelled examples for every class
Decision thresholds must be tuned to the cost of different errors
key_points: Classification predicts discrete classes.
Binary uses sigmoid; multi-class uses softmax; loss is cross-entropy.
Confusion matrix: TP, FP, TN, FN.
Precision = TP/(TP+FP); Recall = TP/(TP+FN); F1 is their harmonic mean.
For imbalanced data prefer precision, recall, F1 or ROC-AUC over accuracy.
viva: What is a confusion matrix?
A table comparing predicted and actual classes, showing true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives.
Define precision and recall.
Precision = TP/(TP+FP), the fraction of predicted positives that are correct. Recall = TP/(TP+FN), the fraction of actual positives that are found.
Why is accuracy misleading for imbalanced data?
If 99% of cases are negative, a model that always predicts negative has 99% accuracy but finds no positives.
Is logistic regression used for regression or classification?
Classification. It outputs a probability using the sigmoid function and applies a threshold, usually 0.5.
interview: In fraud detection, would you optimise precision or recall?

It depends on costs, but usually recall is prioritised because missing a fraud is expensive, while keeping precision acceptable so analysts are not flooded with false alarms. I would look at the precision-recall curve, choose a threshold based on business cost, and report F1 or PR-AUC.
How do you handle class imbalance?

Use suitable metrics (precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC), resample the data (oversampling such as SMOTE, or undersampling), use class weights in the loss, tune the decision threshold, and collect more minority-class data if possible.

mcqs.q: Which function converts scores into probabilities for multi-class classification?
mcqs.explanation: Softmax turns a vector of scores into probabilities that sum to 1.

mcqs.q: Recall is defined as:
mcqs.explanation: Recall measures the fraction of actual positives that were correctly identified.

numerical.problem: A classifier gives TP = 30, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 40. Compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score.
numerical.solution:
Step 1: Total = 30 + 10 + 20 + 40 = 100.
Step 2: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / Total = (30 + 40) / 100 = 0.70.
Step 3: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 30 / 40 = 0.75.
Step 4: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 30 / 50 = 0.60.
Step 5: F1 = 2 * P * R / (P + R) = 2 * 0.75 * 0.60 / 1.35 = 0.667.
Answer: Accuracy 70%, Precision 0.75, Recall 0.60, F1 about 0.67.

topics.name: Clustering (K-Means)
topics.question: What is clustering?
topics.definition: Clustering is an unsupervised learning task that groups data points so that points in the same cluster are more similar to each other than to points in other clusters. K-Means is the most widely used clustering algorithm.
topics.simple: Clustering puts similar things together without being told the groups in advance. K-Means does it by choosing k centre points, assigning each data point to its nearest centre, moving each centre to the average of its points, and repeating until nothing changes.
topics.eli10: Imagine a playground where kids naturally gather in groups: some near the swings, some near the slide, some near the sandbox. If you had to find these groups from a photo, you would look at who is standing close together. Clustering is the computer finding those groups.
topics.analogy: K-Means is like placing k ice-cream stalls on a beach. Each visitor walks to the nearest stall. Then each stall owner moves to the middle of their customers. People switch to whichever stall is now nearest, and the owners move again, until the stalls stop moving. Each stall's customers form a cluster.
how_it_works: Choose the number of clusters k and initialise k centroids (k-means++ is a good initialisation).
Assignment step: assign each point to the nearest centroid, usually by Euclidean distance.
Update step: move each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it.
Repeat assignment and update until assignments stop changing.
Choose k using the elbow method or silhouette score.
topics.example: Points: (1,1), (1,2), (8,8), (9,8) with k = 2 and initial centroids (1,1) and (8,8). The first two points join cluster 1 and the last two join cluster 2. New centroids are (1, 1.5) and (8.5, 8). Assignments no longer change, so the algorithm stops.
applications: Customer segmentation
Image compression by colour quantisation
Grouping similar documents or news articles
Anomaly detection (points far from every cluster)
advantages: K-Means is simple, fast and scales to large datasets
Easy to interpret using centroids
Needs no labels
limitations: k must be chosen in advance
Sensitive to initialisation, outliers and feature scaling
K-Means assumes roughly spherical, similar-sized clusters; DBSCAN handles arbitrary shapes
key_points: Clustering groups similar unlabelled points.
K-Means alternates assignment and centroid-update steps.
It minimises within-cluster sum of squares (inertia).
Choose k with the elbow method or silhouette score.
Other methods: hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN, Gaussian mixture models.
viva: What does K represent in K-Means?
The number of clusters the algorithm should form.
What is the elbow method?
A way to choose k: plot inertia against k and pick the point where adding more clusters stops giving a big improvement (the 'elbow').
Why should features be scaled before K-Means?
Because it uses distances; a feature with a large range would dominate the distance calculation.
How is DBSCAN different from K-Means?
DBSCAN groups dense regions, does not need k, can find arbitrarily shaped clusters and marks outliers as noise.
interview: K-Means gives different results each time you run it. Why, and how do you fix it?

Because centroids are initialised randomly and K-Means converges to a local minimum. Use k-means++ initialisation, run several initialisations (n_init) and keep the solution with the lowest inertia, and fix the random seed for reproducibility.
How is the silhouette score computed?

For each point, a is the mean distance to points in its own cluster and b is the mean distance to points in the nearest other cluster. The silhouette is (b - a) / max(a, b), ranging from -1 to 1; higher means better-separated clusters. The overall score is the average over points.

mcqs.q: K-Means updates each centroid to:
options: The mean of the points assigned to it
mcqs.explanation: The update step moves the centroid to the average of its cluster members.

mcqs.q: Which clustering algorithm does NOT need the number of clusters in advance?
mcqs.explanation: DBSCAN finds clusters based on density using eps and min_samples.

numerical.problem: In K-Means, a cluster contains the points (2, 3), (4, 5) and (6, 7). What is the new centroid after the update step?
numerical.solution:
Step 1: Mean of x-coordinates = (2 + 4 + 6) / 3 = 4.
Step 2: Mean of y-coordinates = (3 + 5 + 7) / 3 = 5.
Answer: The new centroid is (4, 5).

topics.name: Decision Trees
topics.question: What is a decision tree?
topics.definition: A decision tree is a supervised learning model that predicts a target by learning a sequence of if-then questions about the features. Internal nodes test a feature, branches are outcomes and leaves give the prediction.
topics.simple: A decision tree works like the game '20 Questions'. It asks a question about the data, such as 'Is income greater than 50,000?', then follows the yes or no branch and asks the next question, until it reaches an answer. It chooses the questions that best separate the classes, using measures like Gini impurity or entropy.
topics.eli10: Think of a flowchart to decide whether to go outside and play. Is it raining? If yes, stay in. If no, is it too hot? If yes, go to the pool; if no, play football. A decision tree is a flowchart like this that the computer builds by itself from examples.
topics.analogy: A decision tree is like a doctor's diagnostic checklist. The doctor asks the most informative question first ('Do you have a fever?'), then narrows down with more specific questions until reaching a diagnosis. The tree learns which questions to ask, and in which order, from past patient records.
how_it_works: Start with all training data at the root node.
For each feature and threshold, measure how well a split separates the targets (Gini impurity, entropy/information gain, or variance for regression).
Choose the best split and create child nodes.
Repeat recursively until a stopping rule applies (max depth, minimum samples, pure node).
Prune the tree or limit depth to avoid overfitting.
topics.example: Loan approval: the tree first splits on 'credit score > 700'. If yes, it checks 'income > 40,000' and approves if true. If the credit score is 700 or less, it checks 'existing debt < 10,000'. A new applicant with score 720 and income 55,000 follows the left branches and is approved.
applications: Loan and credit approval
Medical decision support
Customer churn prediction
As building blocks for random forests and gradient boosting
advantages: Easy to understand and visualise
Handles numerical and categorical data with little preprocessing (no scaling needed)
Captures non-linear relationships and feature interactions
limitations: Deep trees overfit easily
Unstable: small data changes can produce a very different tree
Greedy splitting does not guarantee the globally best tree
key_points: A decision tree is a flowchart of feature tests leading to predictions.
Splits are chosen by Gini impurity or information gain (entropy reduction).
Gini = 1 - sum(p_i^2); Entropy = -sum(p_i * log2 p_i).
Control overfitting with max_depth, min_samples_leaf and pruning.
Ensembles (random forest, gradient boosting) fix much of a single tree's instability.
viva: What is Gini impurity?
A measure of how mixed the classes in a node are: Gini = 1 - sum of squared class probabilities. It is 0 for a pure node.
What is information gain?
The reduction in entropy after splitting a node on a feature. The split with the highest information gain is chosen.
Why do decision trees overfit?
Because they can keep splitting until every leaf is pure, memorising noise in the training data.
What is pruning?
Removing branches that add little predictive power, to reduce overfitting and simplify the tree.
interview: Why don't decision trees require feature scaling?
Each split compares one feature with a threshold, so only the ordering of values matters, not their scale. Multiplying a feature by 1000 just moves the threshold.
How would you prevent a decision tree from overfitting?

Limit max_depth, set min_samples_split or min_samples_leaf, use cost-complexity pruning, and validate with cross-validation. Often the best fix is to use an ensemble like a random forest or gradient boosting.

mcqs.q: The Gini impurity of a node containing only one class is:
mcqs.explanation: A pure node has Gini = 1 - 1^2 = 0.

mcqs.q: Which is a common way to reduce overfitting in decision trees?
mcqs.explanation: Pruning removes branches that do not improve generalisation.

numerical.problem: A node contains 6 positive and 4 negative examples. Calculate its Gini impurity and entropy.

topics.name: Random Forest
topics.question: What is a random forest?
topics.definition: A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees. Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample of the data and considers a random subset of features at each split; the forest predicts by majority vote (classification) or averaging (regression).
topics.simple: One decision tree can make silly mistakes, but many different trees voting together are much more reliable. A random forest builds hundreds of trees, each trained on a slightly different random sample of the data and features, and combines their votes. This makes it more accurate and much less likely to overfit.
topics.eli10: If you ask one friend to guess how many sweets are in a jar, they might be way off. If you ask 100 friends and take the average, the answer is usually very close. A random forest asks lots of decision trees and combines their answers.
topics.analogy: A random forest is like a panel of doctors who each studied slightly different patient records and focus on different symptoms. Each gives a diagnosis, and the panel goes with the majority. Individual doctors make errors, but their errors differ, so the group decision is more reliable.
how_it_works: Draw a bootstrap sample (sampling with replacement) of the training data for each tree - this is bagging.
Grow a decision tree on it; at every split consider only a random subset of features (e.g. sqrt of total features).
Repeat to build many trees (n_estimators).
Predict by majority vote for classification or the average for regression.
Use out-of-bag samples (not drawn for a tree) to estimate accuracy without a separate validation set.
topics.example: Predicting customer churn with 20 features: a random forest of 300 trees, each using about 4 random features per split. For one customer, 210 trees vote 'will churn' and 90 vote 'will stay', so the forest predicts churn with estimated probability 0.7. Feature importance shows 'monthly charges' and 'contract type' matter most.
applications: Credit risk and fraud detection
Customer churn prediction
Medical outcome prediction
Feature importance analysis on tabular data
advantages: High accuracy on tabular data with little tuning
Reduces the overfitting of single trees (lower variance)
Gives feature importance scores and out-of-bag error estimates
limitations: Less interpretable than a single tree
Larger memory and slower prediction with many trees
Cannot extrapolate beyond the range of training targets in regression
key_points: Random forest = bagging + random feature selection over many decision trees.
Combining de-correlated trees reduces variance.
Prediction: majority vote (classification) or mean (regression).
Out-of-bag error gives a built-in validation estimate.
Key hyper-parameters: n_estimators, max_depth, max_features.
viva: What is bagging?
Bootstrap aggregating: training several models on random samples drawn with replacement and combining their predictions.
Why does a random forest select random features at each split?
To make the trees less correlated; averaging de-correlated trees reduces variance more effectively.
What is out-of-bag error?
The error measured on training samples that were not included in a tree's bootstrap sample, used as a built-in validation estimate.
Does random forest reduce bias or variance?
Mainly variance. Each tree has low bias but high variance; averaging many trees lowers variance.
interview: What is the difference between random forest and gradient boosting?

Random forest builds trees independently in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages them, mainly reducing variance. Gradient boosting builds shallow trees sequentially, where each tree corrects the errors of the previous ones, mainly reducing bias. Boosting is often more accurate but needs more careful tuning and is more prone to overfitting.
How is feature importance computed in a random forest?

Impurity-based importance sums the decrease in Gini or entropy from splits on each feature across all trees. Permutation importance shuffles a feature and measures the drop in performance, which is more reliable when features have many unique values.

mcqs.q: A random forest combines trees using:
mcqs.explanation: Classification uses a vote and regression uses the mean prediction.

mcqs.q: Random forest mainly reduces:
mcqs.explanation: Averaging many high-variance trees lowers the ensemble's variance.

topics.name: Support Vector Machine (SVM)
topics.question: What is a Support Vector Machine (SVM)?
topics.definition: A Support Vector Machine is a supervised learning algorithm that finds the hyperplane separating classes with the maximum margin. The closest training points to the hyperplane are the support vectors. With kernels, SVMs can learn non-linear boundaries.
topics.simple: An SVM tries to draw the widest possible 'street' between two classes. The street's middle line is the decision boundary, and the points touching the edges of the street are called support vectors. A wide street means the classifier is confident and generalises better. If the data cannot be separated by a straight line, the kernel trick lets SVM draw curved boundaries.
topics.eli10: Imagine red and blue marbles on a table and you need to put a stick between them. You want the stick placed so it is as far as possible from the nearest red and nearest blue marble. That way, if a new marble rolls in, you are less likely to put it on the wrong side. That is what an SVM does.
topics.analogy: SVM is like building a road between two villages that must stay as far from both as possible. Only the houses closest to the road (support vectors) determine where it goes; houses far away do not matter. The kernel trick is like lifting the map into 3D so that villages that were tangled together can be separated by a flat sheet.
how_it_works: Represent each example as a point in feature space with label +1 or -1.
Find the hyperplane w.x + b = 0 that maximises the margin 2/||w||.
Soft margin: parameter C trades off margin width against misclassified training points.
Kernel trick: replace dot products with a kernel K(x, x') (linear, polynomial, RBF) to get non-linear boundaries.
Classify new points by the sign of w.x + b.
topics.example: Classifying emails as spam using TF-IDF features: text data is high-dimensional and often almost linearly separable, so a linear SVM works very well. For a dataset shaped like two concentric circles, a linear SVM fails but an RBF-kernel SVM finds a circular boundary.
applications: Text classification and spam detection
Image classification with hand-crafted features
Bioinformatics, e.g. protein classification
Handwriting recognition
advantages: Effective in high-dimensional spaces
Maximum margin gives good generalisation
Kernels allow flexible non-linear boundaries
limitations: Training is slow on very large datasets (roughly quadratic or worse in samples)
Sensitive to the choice of kernel, C and gamma, and to feature scaling
Does not directly output probabilities
key_points: SVM finds the maximum-margin separating hyperplane.
Support vectors are the training points closest to the boundary.
Margin width = 2/||w||.
C controls the soft-margin trade-off; gamma controls RBF kernel width.
The kernel trick computes similarities in a high-dimensional space without explicitly mapping to it.
viva: What are support vectors?
The training points closest to the decision boundary. They alone determine the position of the hyperplane.
What is the kernel trick?
Computing dot products in a high-dimensional feature space through a kernel function, without explicitly transforming the data, so linear methods can learn non-linear boundaries.
What does the C parameter do?
It controls the penalty for misclassification. Large C gives a narrow margin with few training errors; small C allows a wider margin with more errors.
Name three common kernels.
Linear, polynomial and radial basis function (RBF/Gaussian).
interview: When would you choose an SVM over a neural network?

When the dataset is small to medium sized and high-dimensional, like text features, where SVMs train reliably with strong generalisation and few hyper-parameters. For very large datasets or raw images, audio and text, neural networks usually win.
What happens if gamma is too high in an RBF SVM?

Each training point's influence becomes very local, so the boundary wraps tightly around individual points and the model overfits. Too low gamma makes the boundary overly smooth and underfits. Tune gamma and C together with cross-validation.

mcqs.q: SVM chooses the hyperplane that:
mcqs.explanation: SVM is a maximum-margin classifier.

mcqs.q: Which technique allows SVMs to learn non-linear boundaries?
mcqs.explanation: Kernels implicitly map data into a higher-dimensional space.

numerical.problem: A linear SVM has weight vector w = (3, 4). What is the width of its margin?
numerical.solution:
Step 1: ||w|| = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(25) = 5.
Step 2: Margin width = 2 / ||w|| = 2 / 5 = 0.4.
Answer: The margin width is 0.4 units.

topics.name: K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN)
topics.question: What is the K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN) algorithm?
topics.definition: K-Nearest Neighbours is a simple, instance-based supervised learning algorithm. To predict a new point, it finds the k closest training points by a distance measure and takes a majority vote (classification) or average (regression) of their labels.
topics.simple: KNN says 'you are like your neighbours'. To classify a new point, it looks at the k training points closest to it. If most of them are 'cat', it predicts 'cat'. There is no real training phase; the algorithm just stores the data and does the work at prediction time.
topics.eli10: If you move to a new school and want to guess which sports club is most popular, you could ask the five kids sitting closest to you. If three say football, you guess football. KNN guesses the answer by asking the closest examples.
topics.analogy: KNN is like judging a restaurant by looking at the ratings of the k most similar restaurants you already know: same cuisine, price and area. You do not build a general theory of restaurants; you just compare with your nearest known examples.
how_it_works: Store all training examples (lazy learning - no model is fitted).
Scale the features so every feature contributes fairly to distance.
For a new point, compute its distance (Euclidean, Manhattan...) to every training point.
Select the k nearest points.
Predict by majority vote (classification) or average (regression), optionally weighted by distance.
topics.example: Classify a fruit with weight 150 g and sweetness 7 when k = 3. The 3 nearest known fruits are 2 apples and 1 orange, so KNN predicts apple. With k = 1, only the single closest fruit decides, which is more sensitive to noise.
applications: Recommendation systems (similar users or items)
Pattern recognition such as handwritten digits
Missing-value imputation
Simple baselines for classification tasks
advantages: Very simple to understand and implement
No training time
Naturally handles multi-class problems and non-linear boundaries
limitations: Slow prediction on large datasets because it compares with every stored point
Requires feature scaling and suffers from the curse of dimensionality
Sensitive to the choice of k and to noisy or irrelevant features
key_points: KNN is a lazy, instance-based learner.
Prediction uses the k closest training examples.
Small k: low bias, high variance (overfits). Large k: smoother, may underfit.
Always scale features; choose an odd k for binary classification to avoid ties.
KD-trees or approximate nearest-neighbour search speed up prediction.
viva: Why is KNN called a lazy learner?
Because it does not build a model during training; it stores the data and does all computation at prediction time.
What happens when k is very small?
The prediction depends on very few points, so the model is sensitive to noise and tends to overfit.
Why is feature scaling important for KNN?
KNN uses distances, so features with larger ranges would dominate if not scaled.
What is the curse of dimensionality?
In high dimensions, points become far apart and distances become less meaningful, which hurts distance-based methods like KNN.
interview: How do you choose k in KNN?

Try a range of values using cross-validation and pick the k with the best validation score. A common starting point is around the square root of the number of samples, and an odd k avoids ties in binary classification.
How would you make KNN fast for a million data points?
Use spatial indexes like KD-trees or ball trees for low dimensions, and approximate nearest-neighbour libraries such as FAISS or HNSW for high dimensions. Reducing dimensionality with PCA also helps.

mcqs.q: KNN is best described as:
mcqs.explanation: KNN stores training data and defers computation until prediction.

mcqs.q: Increasing k in KNN generally:
mcqs.explanation: More neighbours average out noise, giving a smoother decision boundary.

numerical.problem: Using KNN with k = 3, classify the point P = (2, 3). Training points: A = (1, 3) class Red, B = (2, 5) class Blue, C = (3, 3) class Red, D = (6, 6) class Blue. Use Euclidean distance.
numerical.solution:
Step 1: d(P, A) = sqrt((2-1)^2 + (3-3)^2) = 1.
Step 2: d(P, B) = sqrt(0^2 + 2^2) = 2.
Step 3: d(P, C) = sqrt(1^2 + 0^2) = 1.
Step 4: d(P, D) = sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = 5.
Step 5: The 3 nearest are A (Red), C (Red) and B (Blue).
Answer: Majority vote is Red, so P is classified as Red.

topics.name: Gradient Descent
topics.question: What is gradient descent?
topics.definition: Gradient descent is an iterative optimisation algorithm that minimises a loss function by repeatedly moving the parameters in the direction of the negative gradient: theta = theta - learning_rate * gradient of the loss.
topics.simple: Gradient descent is how most machine learning models learn. The loss tells us how wrong the model is. The gradient tells us which direction makes the loss increase fastest, so we take a small step in the opposite direction. We repeat this many times until the loss stops decreasing. The step size is called the learning rate.
topics.eli10: Imagine you are standing on a foggy hill and want to reach the bottom. You cannot see far, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. So you take a small step downhill, feel again, and take another step. Keep doing this and you reach the valley. That is gradient descent.
topics.analogy: Gradient descent is like adjusting the volume knob of a radio to remove static when you cannot see the dial. You turn it slightly, listen whether it got better or worse, and keep turning in the direction that improves the sound. Turning too fast (large learning rate) makes you overshoot; too slowly takes forever.
how_it_works: Initialise the parameters (weights) randomly or to zero.
Compute the loss on the data (or a mini-batch).
Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to each parameter.
Update: w = w - learning_rate * gradient.
Repeat for many iterations/epochs until convergence.
topics.example: Minimise f(w) = (w - 3)^2 starting at w = 0 with learning rate 0.1. The gradient is 2(w - 3) = -6, so w becomes 0 - 0.1 * (-6) = 0.6. Next the gradient is -4.8 and w becomes 1.08. Each step moves w closer to the minimum at w = 3.
applications: Training linear and logistic regression
Training neural networks (together with backpropagation)
Fine-tuning large language models
Matrix factorisation for recommender systems
advantages: Simple and general: works for any differentiable loss
Scales to millions or billions of parameters with mini-batches
Many improved variants (Momentum, RMSProp, Adam)
limitations: Choosing the learning rate is critical
Can get stuck in local minima or saddle points for non-convex losses
Slow convergence on badly scaled or ill-conditioned problems
key_points: Update rule: w = w - learning_rate * dLoss/dw.
Batch GD uses all data; stochastic GD uses one example; mini-batch GD uses small batches.
Too large a learning rate diverges; too small converges slowly.
Adam combines momentum and adaptive per-parameter learning rates.
Learning-rate schedules (warm-up, cosine decay) improve training.
viva: What is the learning rate?
A hyper-parameter that controls the size of each parameter update in gradient descent.
What is the difference between batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent?
Batch GD computes the gradient on the whole dataset, SGD on a single example and mini-batch GD on a small subset. Mini-batch is the standard compromise between stability and speed.
What happens if the learning rate is too high?
Updates overshoot the minimum; the loss oscillates or diverges.
What is momentum?
An extension that accumulates a moving average of past gradients, which speeds up movement in consistent directions and damps oscillations.
interview: Why is Adam so widely used?

Adam keeps a moving average of gradients (momentum) and of squared gradients, and uses them to give each parameter its own adaptive step size. It works well with little tuning, handles sparse and noisy gradients, and is the default for training transformers. SGD with momentum can generalise slightly better in some vision tasks.
Your training loss is going up instead of down. What would you check?

First the learning rate, which is the most common cause, so I would lower it or add warm-up. Then check for bugs: the sign of the update, labels matching inputs, loss computation, data normalisation, and exploding gradients, for which gradient clipping helps.

mcqs.q: In gradient descent, parameters are updated in the direction of:
mcqs.explanation: Moving against the gradient decreases the loss.

mcqs.q: If the learning rate is too large, the loss will most likely:
mcqs.explanation: Large steps overshoot the minimum.

mcqs.q: Which variant uses a small subset of data per update?
mcqs.explanation: Mini-batch gradient descent uses small batches such as 32 or 64 examples.

numerical.problem: Minimise the loss L(w) = w^2 using gradient descent with learning rate 0.1, starting at w = 5. Compute w after two updates.
numerical.solution:
Step 1: The gradient is dL/dw = 2w.
Step 2: Update 1: gradient = 2 * 5 = 10, so w = 5 - 0.1 * 10 = 4.
Step 3: Update 2: gradient = 2 * 4 = 8, so w = 4 - 0.1 * 8 = 3.2.
Answer: After two updates w = 3.2, moving towards the minimum at w = 0.

troubleshooting.problem: My model's training loss becomes NaN after a few iterations. What is wrong?
troubleshooting.solution:
A NaN loss usually means the optimisation is numerically unstable. Check these in order:
1. Learning rate too high - reduce it by 10x or add a warm-up schedule.
2. Exploding gradients - add gradient clipping (e.g. max norm 1.0).
3. Invalid operations - log(0) or division by zero in a custom loss; add a small epsilon.
4. Bad input data - check for NaN or infinite values and normalise features.
5. Mixed precision overflow - fp16 can overflow; use bf16 or loss scaling.

topics.name: Overfitting
topics.question: What is overfitting?
topics.definition: Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data too closely, including its noise, so it performs very well on training data but poorly on new, unseen data. It is a sign of high variance.
topics.simple: Overfitting is when a model memorises instead of learning. It gets almost perfect scores on the data it was trained on, but it fails on new data because it learned details and noise that do not generalise. You can spot it when training accuracy keeps improving while validation accuracy gets worse.
topics.eli10: Imagine a student who memorises the exact answers to last year's exam instead of understanding the lessons. If this year's questions are slightly different, the student is stuck. A model that overfits is like that student: great at the old questions, bad at new ones.
topics.analogy: Overfitting is like a tailor who makes a suit that fits one customer so perfectly it even follows the wrinkles in their shirt on that particular day. It will not fit anyone else, and it will not even fit the same customer tomorrow.
how_it_works: The model has too much capacity (too many parameters or too deep) relative to the data.
During training, it reduces training loss by fitting noise and quirks of individual examples.
Validation loss stops improving and starts rising while training loss keeps falling.
Detect it by comparing training and validation performance (learning curves).
Fix it with regularisation, more data, simpler models, early stopping, dropout or augmentation.
topics.example: A degree-15 polynomial fitted to 10 noisy points passes through every point (training error close to 0) but wiggles wildly between them, so its test error is huge. A straight line or degree-2 curve has a small training error but predicts new points much better.
applications: Diagnosing model performance through learning curves
Choosing model complexity and regularisation strength
Deciding when to stop training (early stopping)
Fine-tuning LLMs on small datasets, where overfitting is a real risk
advantages: Understanding overfitting guides model selection
Clear diagnostic: training vs validation gap
Well-known, effective remedies exist
limitations: An overfit model gives falsely optimistic training results
It generalises poorly and can fail in production
Removing it completely may cause underfitting; a balance is needed
key_points: Overfitting = low training error, high validation/test error (high variance).
Causes: model too complex, too little data, training too long, noisy features.
Remedies: more data, augmentation, L1/L2 regularisation, dropout, early stopping, simpler model.
Cross-validation gives a reliable estimate of generalisation.
It is one side of the bias-variance trade-off; underfitting is the other.
viva: How can you detect overfitting?
By comparing training and validation performance: a large gap, with high training accuracy and much lower validation accuracy, indicates overfitting.
Give two methods to reduce overfitting.
Regularisation such as L2 weight decay or dropout, and getting more training data or using data augmentation. Early stopping is another.
What is early stopping?
Stopping training when validation loss stops improving, before the model starts to memorise training data.
How does dropout reduce overfitting?
It randomly switches off neurons during training, so the network cannot rely on any single neuron and learns more robust features.
interview: Your model has 99% training accuracy and 70% validation accuracy. What do you do?

This is overfitting. I would first check for data leakage or a distribution mismatch between the splits. Then I would reduce model complexity, add regularisation such as weight decay or dropout, use data augmentation or collect more data, apply early stopping, and use cross-validation to confirm the improvement.
Explain the bias-variance trade-off.

Bias is error from overly simple assumptions, which causes underfitting. Variance is error from sensitivity to the particular training set, which causes overfitting. Increasing model complexity lowers bias but raises variance, so we pick the complexity that minimises total validation error.

mcqs.q: A model with very low training error but high test error is:
mcqs.explanation: The gap between training and test error is the hallmark of overfitting.

mcqs.q: Which technique does NOT help reduce overfitting?
mcqs.explanation: More parameters increase capacity and usually make overfitting worse.

troubleshooting.problem: My training accuracy is 99% but my validation accuracy is only 70%. How do I fix it?
troubleshooting.solution:
This large gap means the model is overfitting. Try these steps:
1. Check for data problems first - leakage, duplicates across splits, or different distributions.
2. Add regularisation - weight decay (L2) and dropout.
3. Use data augmentation or collect more training data.
4. Reduce model complexity - fewer layers, units or tree depth.
5. Use early stopping based on validation loss.
6. Confirm the improvement with cross-validation rather than a single split.

topics.name: Underfitting
topics.question: What is underfitting?
topics.definition: Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern in the data, so it performs poorly on both the training data and new data. It is a sign of high bias.
topics.simple: Underfitting is when a model has not learned enough. It makes big errors even on the training data, because it is too simple or was not trained long enough. For example, trying to fit a straight line to data that clearly follows a curve.
topics.eli10: Imagine trying to draw a picture of a cat using only one straight line. No matter how you place the line, it will not look like a cat. The drawing tool is too simple. That is underfitting: the model is too simple to show the real pattern.
topics.analogy: Underfitting is like summarising an entire novel as 'some things happened'. It is never exactly wrong, but it misses all the important details, so it is useless for answering questions about the story.
how_it_works: The model's capacity is too low or its features are not informative enough.
Both training and validation errors stay high and close to each other.
It may also happen if training stops too early or regularisation is too strong.
Detect it with learning curves: both curves plateau at a high error.
Fix it with a more complex model, better features, longer training or weaker regularisation.
topics.example: Predicting salary from years of experience when salary actually grows quickly at first and then levels off. A straight line misses the curve and gives training R^2 = 0.55 and test R^2 = 0.53. A polynomial or tree-based model captures the curve and raises both scores.
applications: Diagnosing learning curves
Deciding to increase model capacity or improve features
Tuning regularisation strength
Checking whether training ran long enough
advantages: Easy to detect: training error itself is high
Usually easy to fix by adding capacity or features
Underfit models are simple and stable, which can be useful as baselines
limitations: Poor accuracy everywhere
Misses important relationships in the data
Adding too much capacity to fix it can lead to overfitting
key_points: Underfitting = high training error and high test error (high bias).
Causes: model too simple, poor features, too much regularisation, too little training.
Remedies: more complex model, feature engineering, less regularisation, longer training.
Opposite of overfitting in the bias-variance trade-off.
Learning curves show both errors high and close together.
viva: How is underfitting different from overfitting?
Underfitting means the model performs poorly even on training data (high bias); overfitting means it performs well on training data but poorly on new data (high variance).
Give two causes of underfitting.
A model that is too simple for the data, and excessive regularisation. Training for too few epochs is another cause.
How can you fix underfitting?
Use a more complex model, add better features, reduce regularisation or train for longer.
interview: Both your training and validation accuracy are around 60%. What is happening and what do you do?

Both are low and close, so the model is underfitting. I would increase capacity with a deeper network or a non-linear model, engineer more informative features, reduce regularisation, train longer with a well-tuned learning rate, and verify the labels are correct, since noisy labels also cap performance.

mcqs.q: Underfitting is associated with:
mcqs.explanation: An underfit model makes strong, overly simple assumptions.

mcqs.q: Which change can reduce underfitting?
mcqs.explanation: More capacity lets the model capture the pattern.

troubleshooting.problem: My model has high error on both the training and test sets. What should I do?
troubleshooting.solution:
High error on both sets means the model is underfitting (high bias). Try:
1. A more expressive model - more layers or units, or a non-linear algorithm.
2. Better features - add interactions, polynomial terms or domain features.
3. Less regularisation - lower weight decay or dropout.
4. Longer training with a properly tuned learning rate.
5. Check the data - noisy or wrong labels limit what any model can learn.

topics.name: Artificial Neural Network (ANN)
topics.question: What is an artificial neural network?
topics.definition: An artificial neural network (ANN) is a model made of layers of connected neurons. Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and applies a non-linear activation function. Stacking layers lets the network learn complex functions from data.
topics.simple: A neural network is a stack of simple calculators called neurons. Each neuron takes some numbers, multiplies them by weights, adds them up and passes the result through an activation function. The input layer receives the data, hidden layers find patterns, and the output layer gives the prediction. Training adjusts the weights so the predictions become correct.
topics.eli10: Imagine a team of friends passing notes. The first friends look at a picture and each notices something small, like a line or a colour. They pass notes to the next friends, who combine them into bigger ideas like 'ear' or 'whisker'. The last friend says 'cat!'. A neural network is a team like that, and it learns which notes matter most.
topics.analogy: A neural network is like a company's decision process. Front-line staff (input layer) collect raw information, middle managers (hidden layers) combine it into summaries, and the CEO (output layer) makes the final decision. Training is like performance reviews: whoever contributed to a wrong decision has their influence (weights) adjusted.
how_it_works: Input layer receives the features, e.g. pixel values.
Each neuron computes z = w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + b, then a = activation(z).
Hidden layers transform the representation step by step (forward propagation).
The output layer produces predictions; a loss function measures the error.
Backpropagation computes gradients and gradient descent updates all weights.
topics.example: Handwritten digit recognition (MNIST): each 28x28 image becomes 784 inputs. A network with one hidden layer of 128 ReLU neurons and an output layer of 10 softmax neurons (one per digit) can reach about 97-98% test accuracy after a few epochs.
applications: Image and speech recognition
Tabular prediction such as credit scoring
Recommendation systems
As the building block of CNNs, RNNs and transformers
advantages: Can approximate very complex, non-linear functions
Learns features automatically from raw data
Scales well with more data and compute
limitations: Needs lots of data and compute
Hard to interpret (black box)
Many hyper-parameters; prone to overfitting without regularisation
key_points: Neuron: weighted sum + bias, then a non-linear activation.
Layers: input, one or more hidden layers, output.
Forward propagation computes predictions; backpropagation computes gradients.
Without non-linear activations, stacked layers collapse into one linear model.
Universal approximation: a wide enough network can approximate any continuous function.
viva: What is a perceptron?
The simplest neural network unit: it computes a weighted sum of inputs plus bias and applies a step function to output a class. A single perceptron can only learn linearly separable problems.
Why do we need activation functions?
They introduce non-linearity. Without them, any number of layers is equivalent to a single linear transformation.
What is a hidden layer?
A layer between input and output whose neurons learn intermediate representations of the data.
Why can't a single perceptron solve XOR?
XOR is not linearly separable, and a single perceptron can only draw one straight line. A network with a hidden layer can solve it.
What is an epoch?
